answer:
**SVD decomposes a linear map into rotation, axis scaling, and another rotation/reflection.** For a rectangular matrix A, the right singular vectors describe input directions, singular values describe their nonnegative amplification, and left singular vectors describe the corresponding output directions. This works even when A is not square and ordinary eigenvectors are not the appropriate tool. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html)

**Why small singular values can be dropped.** If one direction is scaled strongly and another barely at all, the latter contributes little to the matrix's action under standard norm criteria. Keeping only the largest k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm and, with the appropriate statement, spectral norm. This is the Eckart–Young–Mirsky result.

For centered data, PCA uses right singular vectors as principal feature directions. Squared singular values divided by N-1 give sample explained variances. Without centering, the decomposition is still an SVD, but it is not the usual mean-centered PCA interpretation.

**A compression example.** A nearly rank-one image matrix may be well approximated by one outer product of a column pattern and row pattern. More retained components add detail, with a measurable reconstruction-error tradeoff.

The largest-variance directions need not be the most predictive of a label, and small singular values can still matter for a particular downstream task. Choose rank using the actual objective and validation, not only a convenient explained-variance percentage.

**Technical details and references.**

SVD writes an $m\times n$ matrix as $U\Sigma V^T$ with orthonormal singular vectors and nonnegative singular values. It exists even for rectangular or nonsymmetric matrices. Keeping the top $k$ singular terms gives the best rank-$k$ approximation in Frobenius norm and spectral norm. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html)

$$A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_iv_i^T,\qquad \|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2.$$

For a centered data matrix, right singular vectors are PCA directions and scores are $U\Sigma$. Covariance eigenvalues are $\sigma_i^2/(N-1)$ under sample-covariance normalization. Centering and scaling choices change PCA. Repeated singular values can make individual basis vectors nonunique even when the retained subspace is well defined.
